prompt.context: Your interviewer asks you to estimate the number of gas stations in the city of Chicago.
prompt.question: Estimate the number of gas stations in the city of Chicago. (1) Think about all the ways you would go about estimating this and describe them. (2) Choose one method and do the estimate. (3) A friend of yours wants to open a gas station in Chicago — what things would you suggest your friend consider?

framework: Approach 1 — Density/block method: Use a known city (e.g., Philadelphia) as a benchmark. Estimate gas stations per block, then estimate total city blocks to get total gas stations.
Approach 2 — Demand/throughput method: Estimate population → cars → gallons consumed per year → gallons sold per station per year → number of stations needed.
Approach 3 — Transactions method: Estimate average customers per day per station and average tank size to get average sales per store, then back into total stations from total city demand.
For Part 2 (business attractiveness): First assess industry-level attractiveness using a Porter's Five Forces or similar lens, then assess the specific opportunity.

questions.prompt: Walk through at least two estimation methods for the number of gas stations in Chicago.
questions.guidance: Candidate should articulate multiple approaches before committing to one: (a) density/block benchmark from a known city, (b) population → cars → fuel demand → stations, (c) transactions per station. Should explain the logic of each and why they chose their method.

math.setup: Illustrative demand-based approach: Chicago population ~3M; average household size ~2.5 → ~1.2M households; ~1 car per household → ~1.2M cars. Each car uses ~500 gallons/year (12,000 miles / 24 mpg). Total city demand = 1.2M × 500 = 600M gallons/year. A typical gas station sells ~1M gallons/year (roughly 1,000 customers/day × 25 gallons × 365 days ≈ 9M gal — scale down for realistic utilization; casebook suggests ~1M as a reasonable estimate). Stations = 600M / 1M = 600 stations.
math.answer: Approximately 600 gas stations in Chicago (order-of-magnitude; reasonable range 500–800)

questions.prompt: A friend wants to open a gas station in Chicago. What should they consider?
questions.guidance: Strong answer covers two layers: (1) Industry-level attractiveness — margins are low, competition is intense (commoditized product), supplier power is high (large multinational oil companies), buyer power is high (easy to drive to competitor), substitutes are limited but not a major factor. Overall: a difficult industry. (2) Individual opportunity assessment — local competition and whether an area is underserved; location quality and traffic volume; potential for ancillary revenue (convenience store, diesel for trucks); growth prospects (population trends, traffic flow changes).

brainstorming.prompt: What factors would you tell a friend to consider before opening a gas station in Chicago?

categories.name: Industry attractiveness
ideas: Margins are low in gasoline retail
Product is commoditized — price is the primary differentiator
Supplier power is very high (major multinational oil companies)
Buyer power is high — customers can easily drive to the next station
Substitutes (walking, cycling) exist but are not a significant threat

categories.name: Location and local competition
ideas: Volume of traffic near the site
Number of existing gas stations nearby (branded vs. unbranded)
Whether the area is currently underserved
Residential vs. commercial area — affects demand patterns

categories.name: Revenue mix
ideas: Selling diesel fuel for trucks (commercial area)
Attaching a convenience store or small grocery for higher-margin sales
Car wash or other ancillary services

categories.name: Growth prospects
ideas: Will traffic flows change (new roads, development)?
Trend toward electric vehicles as a long-term risk

recommendation: Overall, the gas station industry is structurally unattractive: low margins, high competition, high supplier and buyer power.

Entry should only be pursued if there is a compelling individual opportunity — specifically an underserved high-traffic location with meaningful ancillary revenue potential (e.g., a well-sized convenience store).
risks: Ongoing margin pressure from branded competitors and oil price volatility
Rising EV adoption could reduce long-term fuel demand
High capital cost of environmental compliance and underground tank maintenance
next_steps: Conduct a site-specific traffic count and competitive mapping for any candidate location
Model unit economics including fuel margin, convenience-store margin, and break-even volume
Assess franchise vs. independent model trade-offs (brand support vs. flexibility)
